title: Koliko je sati?
theme: Clocks and daily rhythm across BiH
reviewerNotes: Revised for BiH geographic diversity (Travnik, Una/Bihać, Neum) and accurate Travnik sahat-kula art. ready for human review.
storyBeat: Emir teaches Ana the time, then shows that Bosnia’s rhythm is bigger than one city: Travnik’s sahat-kula, Una mornings near Bihać, and weekend dreams of Neum.

vocabulary: Parts of day: jutro, podne, popodne, večer
Days: danas, sutra + weekdays ponedjeljak. nedjelja
grammar: Asking and answering the hour with sat/sati
Danas / sutra for today and tomorrow
culture: Sahat-kule (clock towers) in towns across BiH. not only Sarajevo
Travnik under Vlašić; Una near Bihać; Neum on the Adriatic

grammar.title: Koliko je sati?
grammar.explanation: Ask the time with Koliko je sati? Answer with a number from Lesson 3 plus sat or sati. Jedan je sat (1:00). For 2. 4 you will often hear dva/tri/četiri sata in real speech. for this lesson, memorize the friendly pattern X je sati for 5. 12 and Jedan je sat for 1. Also say U osam sati (at eight o’clock) as a chunk.

examples.bosnian: Osam je sati. / U osam sati.
examples.english: It is eight. / At eight o’clock.

grammar.title: Danas and sutra
grammar.explanation: Danas = today. Sutra = tomorrow. Pair them with a weekday: Danas je petak. Sutra je subota. You can also place plans: Sutra u deset sati. kod Amire.

grammar.title: Weekdays. chant the week
grammar.explanation: Learn the seven days as a list: ponedjeljak, utorak, srijeda, četvrtak, petak, subota, nedjelja. Watch četvrtak (č) and srijeda / nedjelja. Do not worry about full case endings yet. say Danas je… + the day name.

culture.title: Time across Bosnia: Travnik’s sahat-kula
culture.body: Ottoman Bosnia left sahat-kule (clock towers) in many towns, not just Sarajevo. Emir’s photo today is Travnik: a stone sahat-kula under the cliffs of Mount Vlašić, once a seat of Ottoman viziers. Sarajevo’s tower by Gazi Husrev-beg’s mosque was famous for lunar prayer time. Travnik keeps a different skyline under the mountain. Day rhythm changes with place too. There is misty jutro on the Una near Bihać, bright inland popodne, and večer plans for Neum on Bosnia’s short Adriatic coast. Learning to ask Koliko je sati also means learning where in the country that hour belongs.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson A: Ask the time
lessonBlocks.body: Drill Koliko je sati? then answer with Lesson 3 numbers: Pet je sati. Osam je sati. Deset je sati. Jedan je sat. Add place chunks: U osam sati (kod Amire. U dvanaest sati) podne. Emir flips a postcard of Travnik’s sahat-kula while Ana practices. the same question works in every Bosnian town. Ana still says Kasno je! when she is late for kahva.

lessonBlocks.title: Lesson B: Days and the week’s plan
lessonBlocks.body: Chant the weekdays twice. Then build real lines: Danas je petak. Sutra je subota. Mark parts of day: jutro, podne, popodne, večer. Emir sketches a wider week on a napkin: subota (Una? nedjelja) Neum san? For now they stay in Sarajevo, but sutra always points somewhere on the map of BiH. End with one plan: Sutra u deset sati, kod Amire!
tips: četvrtak and srijeda need careful letters

conversation.title: Koliko je sati, Emire?
conversation.setting: Outside Amira’s, late afternoon. Ana checks her phone; Emir shows a postcard of Travnik’s clock tower under Vlašić.

lines.speaker: Emir
lines.bosnian: Da. Sutra u deset sati ovdje. Poslije Travnik? Una?
lines.english: Yes. Tomorrow at ten o’clock here. Later Travnik? The Una?

lines.speaker: Amira
lines.bosnian: Dobro. Jutro za kahvu. Subota za rijeku!
lines.english: Good. Morning for coffee. Saturday for the river!

funFacts.title: Travnik and Vlašić
funFacts.body: Travnik was a major Ottoman administrative centre. Its sahat-kula stands with Mount Vlašić behind it. Central Bosnia has its own political history, not a footnote to Sarajevo.

funFacts.title: Many sahat-kule
funFacts.body: Clock towers appear in towns across BiH, including Sarajevo and Travnik. Sarajevo’s tower is often remembered for once tracking lunar prayer time. That detail roots Koliko je sati? in local history.

funFacts.title: Una mornings near Bihać
funFacts.body: In the northwest, the Una River runs clear past Bihać. Locals talk about jutro on the river with the same affection Sarajevo keeps for kahva. Different place, same love of a slow start.

funFacts.title: Neum touches the sea
funFacts.body: BiH has a short Adriatic coastline at Neum. A sutra plan can mean salt air, not only mountain towns. That matters when you practice danas and sutra as real life, not workbook fiction.

civicContext.title: A country with almost no sea door of its own
civicContext.body: Bosnia and Herzegovina’s only coastline is the short stretch at Neum, and most Adriatic freight still depends on access through neighboring Croatia. Croatia’s Pelješac Bridge, opened in 2022, connects Croatian territory around Neum, while BiH traders still face foreign customs regimes rather than a full national deep-water port system. A weekend dream of the coast sits beside that structural fact: the state remains dependent on a neighbor for much of its maritime trade access.
